Title: Addressing the impact of intergenerational pain in Rwanda
NewsSummary: Rwanda's 1994 genocide has grave mental health impacts not only the survivors, but on their offspring also.
NewsContent:
Mental health remains a taboo topic in many societies in Africa and many victims choose to suffer in silence rather than seeking the support they need. In the wake of the Rwandan genocide's 25th anniversary, the topic of mental health continues to gain importance as the concern around intergenerational trauma grows.

The 2016 Youth Survey, conducted by the Aga Khan University's East Africa Institute, found that 78 per cent of Rwanda's population is below the age of 35 years, indicating that most of Rwanda's populace includes genocide survivors as well as those born after the tragic event.

The latter of these two groups is the most affected by the intergenerational pain that has been left behind in the aftermath. The SANA initiative, founded by Laure Iyaga, represents a commitment to deconstruct the stigma around mental health in Rwanda.

The word 'Sana' is a universal word for 'well-being'. In Arabic it is referred to as 'resplendence' or 'brilliance'; in Portuguese, it means 'healthy'; in Latin, the word means 'whole'. In Kinyarwanda, however, 'Sana' is derived from the verb 'Gusana', which means to 'rebuild', 'to restore', and 'to mend'. 

In a recent article for Inzozi Magazine, Iyaga recounts the initial difficulty of starting such an initiative in her communities. "Here, everything pertaining to mental health is systemically equated to dementia (or insanity), so we have to set ourselves the mission to demystify mental health. We need to put an end to this pain which is passed on from one generation to the next because of the lack of appropriate response to it because the feelings our people experience when recalling this tragedy are suppressed. Children should not have to grow up in the shadow of this pain," she says.

Statistics show that 99 percent of genocide survivors witnessed some form of violence and 31 percent of women suffered rape or another form of sexual assault, according to MINECOFIN. In a recent study published by Bar-Ilan University, the children of Tutsi survivors - who were yet to be born during the time of the slaughter - are among those most affected by trauma. As a result, children of survivors tend to experience more symptoms, such as thoughts and nightmares about the genocide, deeper effects on their self-perception, and tend to feel less equipped to handle adverse situations, according to the study.

"We need to understand that genocide and massive trauma can leave their mark not only on survivors who were directly exposed but also on their offspring and probably on other family relatives, as well," says Dr Ben Mollov, a Bar-Ilan political scientist who co-authored the study. "We also know from previous studies that the effects of trauma may extend across several generations and linger for decades after the focal trauma took place. These insights should guide policymakers and clinicians when planning interventions aimed at mitigating the plight of traumatised individuals and their families, particularly in terms of increasing resilience.  This can also bear relevance for improved intergroup relations," said Mollov in an interview with CFBIU.

Since the end of the 1994 genocide, the Rwandan government has created a National Unity and Reconciliation Program. In partnership with various non-governmental organisations, this government-spearheaded initiative aims to establish nationwide healing and to implement national programs that establish peace and unity for many years to come. As various initiatives continue to look at the impacts of trauma passed down to the children of survivors, attention is also being brought to Tutsi survivors who live amongst Hutus and even cases of Tutsis who married Hutus and have openly welcomed them into their families. 

Numbers of reported cases of post-traumatic stress disorder and complex post-traumatic stress disorder remain on the rise, however, Rwanda still remains one of the few countries in Africa to actually implement national policies towards mental health. In doing so, they hope to "heal mental disorders as early as possible, holistically, and close to the person's home and community for the prevention of mental health disorders and mental health promotion," complemented by additional levels of care when needed, according to the Ministry of Health.

SANA continues to be a leading example of an organisation that works within the institutional context of Rwanda, leads campaigns to raise awareness and provides community support. The SANA initiative hopes to carry-on these initiatives around mental health in and beyond Rwanda by expanding its presence to six additional countries in Africa by the end of 2019.

The efforts in Rwanda to address the emotional impacts left by the genocide collectively prove that although pain can be long-lasting, it can be healed.


Nina Plummer is an EAI Research Assistant, conducting research on malnutrition, early childhood development, and learning outcomes.
